mainTopic: Indirect killing and accidental harm: the end of the dispute about killing a person who is already doomed, the ox that gores a falling child (כופר), and רבה's rule about a man who falls from a roof onto a woman
overview: This amud finishes רבה's cases about a child thrown off a roof. The חכמים exempt ten people who each hit one victim, while רבי יהודה בן בתירא makes the last one liable. An ox that catches the falling child depends on whether כופר is the victim's value or the owner's value. רבה then teaches that a man who falls from a roof pays four payments but not בושת, because בושת needs intent. How much a falling man pays depends on whether the wind was usual or unusual, and on whether he twisted to land on the person. רבה also rules that a coal placed on someone's heart brings no liability, but a coal on his garment must be paid for. A slave counts like a person and an ox like property. The פרק כיצד הרגל ends, and the new פרק opens with a משנה about a jug left in רשות הרבים. The גמרא notices that משניות switch between כד and חבית, and רב פפא says the words mean the same thing for buying and selling. The case of a town where most people keep the words apart continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The ten-attackers ברייתא is completed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא that רבה cited ends. The חכמים exempt all the attackers. רבי יהודה בן בתירא says that when they struck one after another, the last one is liable because he brought the death closer.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are exempt. רבי יהודה בן בתירא says: if they hit him one after another, the last one is liable, because he brought his death closer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא it brought as the source for רבה's case of a child thrown off a roof onto someone's sword.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is about ten people who each hit a victim, who then dies. The חכמים say no single person killed him, so all are exempt. רבי יהודה בן בתירא says that when the blows came one after another, the last hitter is liable, because he made the death come sooner. The same reasoning would apply to the person who caught the falling child on his sword.

keyTerms.meaning: He brought his death closer (hastened it)

steps.confusionAlert: The step starts in the middle of a ברייתא. The word 'exempt' refers to the ten attackers from the earlier part of the ברייתא, not to someone new.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up a basic question for indirect killing: is someone who speeds up the death of a person already doomed counted as a killer?

phrases.english: are exempt.
phrases.notes: This ends the ברייתא about ten people hitting one victim. All of them are exempt according to the חכמים.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:
If one after another, the last one is liable,
because he brought his death closer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא that רבה cited, before this section begins, as the source for the case of the child caught on a sword.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's claim that the case of the child caught on a sword depends on a dispute
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of ten people hitting one victim, with the חכמים against רבי יהודה בן בתירא

steps.title: An ox catches the falling child on its horns
steps.stepSummary: רבה gives a parallel case. If the falling child is gored by an ox, whether the owner pays כופר depends on a dispute between רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: If an ox came and caught him on its horns, it depends on the dispute between רבי ישמעאל son of יוחנן בן ברוקא and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new version of the same case, where an ox kills the falling child instead of a person. It says the answer depends on an earlier dispute, and the next step will show that dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When an ox known to be dangerous kills a person, the owner pays כופר (ransom). The question is how to value that payment when the child was already doomed. רבה says this depends on whose value the כופר is based on.

phrases.english: If an ox came and caught him on its horns,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the child who was thrown off the roof in רבה's earlier case.

phrases.english: it is the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael

phrases.aramaic: בְּנוֹ שֶׁל יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָא וְרַבָּנַן,
phrases.english: son of Yoḥanan ben Beroka and the Rabbis,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a person catching the child on a sword to an ox catching the child on its horns.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether the ox's owner owes כופר for the doomed child depends on the dispute between רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא and the רבנן.

steps.title: The ברייתא: whose value is the ransom?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא on 'וְנָתַן פִּדְיֹן נַפְשׁוֹ' records two views. The רבנן say the payment is the victim's value. רבי ישמעאל says it is the value of the owner who caused the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'He shall give the redemption of his life' means the value of the one who was hurt. רבי ישמעאל son of רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא says: the value of the one who caused the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the source of the dispute it just mentioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the רבנן, the owner pays what the victim was worth. A child already falling to his death has no value, so the owner pays nothing. According to רבי ישמעאל, the owner pays his own value, so he pays even here.

keyTerms.meaning: Redemption of his life (the כופר payment)
The value of the one responsible for the damage (the owner)
As it was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: The ox case depends on how כופר is measured. Under the victim's value, a doomed child is worth nothing and the owner is exempt. Under the owner's value, the owner pays.

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'He shall give the redemption of his life' means the value of the injured one.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka, says:
the value of the damager.
phrases.notes: He means the ox's owner. The owner pays what he himself is worth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the ברייתא behind the dispute named in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That the ox case depends on this dispute

steps.title: A man falls from a roof onto a woman
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that a man who falls from a roof and is accidentally inserted into a woman is liable for four payments. If she was his יבמה, he has not acquired her.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: if he fell from the top of the roof and was inserted into a woman, he is liable for four things. And with his יבמה, he did not acquire her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives another case of harm done with no intent: a fall from a roof that ends in accidental relations. He states two rulings, one about payments and one about יבום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even without intent, the man caused harm, so he pays four of the five standard payments. For יבום, an act with no intent at all to have relations does not count as acquiring the יבמה.

keyTerms.meaning: Was inserted (by the force of the fall)
His brother's widow, waiting for יבום
He did not acquire her (the יבום is not done)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rulings. He still owes money for the damage, but the same act does not count as יבום.

phrases.english: And Rabba said:
If he fell from the top of the roof and was inserted into a woman,
he is liable for four things.
And with his yevama, he did not acquire her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling from רבה on the theme of falling from a roof and causing harm without intent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Falling onto a woman obligates four payments, and it does not acquire a יבמה.

steps.title: Which four payments he owes
steps.stepSummary: The four payments are נזק, צער, ריפוי and שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is liable for damage, pain, medical costs, and lost work time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רבה meant by 'four things.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who injures another normally owes five payments. Here four apply, since each of them is owed even when the harm was accidental.

phrases.english: He is liable for damage, for pain, for medical costs, for loss of livelihood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Lists the 'four things' from step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The four payments are נזק, צער, ריפוי and שבת.

steps.title: No payment for humiliation without intent
steps.stepSummary: He does not pay בושת, because a משנה teaches that one is liable for בושת only when he intends to shame.
steps.simpleTranslation: But not for humiliation, as we learned: one is not liable for humiliation unless he intends to.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the fifth payment, בושת, is missing from the list, and proves it from a משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בושת is different from the other four payments: it requires intent. A man who simply fell had no intent, so he owes only four payments.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה

steps.whatToRemember: Four of the five payments apply even to accidental harm. בושת applies only when there was intent.

phrases.english: But humiliation, no,
as we learned: one is not liable for humiliation
unless he intends.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the list in step 5 has only four payments.
steps.raayaObject: That the man who fell is exempt from בושת
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה stating that one is not liable for בושת unless he intends to shame

steps.title: Falling from a roof in different kinds of wind
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that a man who falls from a roof and causes damage and shame pays different amounts depending on the wind. If he twisted his body to land on the person, he even pays בושת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: If a person fell from a roof because of an unusual wind and caused damage and shame, he pays only for the damage and is exempt from the other four payments. If it was a usual wind, he pays the four payments but not for shame. If he turned himself over while falling, he pays for shame too.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a three-level ruling about a man who falls off a roof onto someone. How much he pays goes up as he becomes more responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unusual wind is pure accident, so he pays only נזק. A usual wind is negligence (he should have been careful), so he pays the four payments, but not בושת, because he never meant to hit anyone. If he twisted to land on the person to save himself, he intended to land on him, so he pays בושת as well.

keyTerms.meaning: An unusual wind that no one would expect
A usual, ordinary wind that a person should watch out for

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'four things' means different payments in the two cases. In the unusual wind case he is exempt from the four besides נזק (צער, ריפוי, שבת, בושת). In the usual wind case he pays four (נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת) but not בושת.

phrases.english: And רבה said:
If one fell from the top of the roof
because of an unusual wind,
and he caused damage and shame,
he is liable for the damage,
and exempt from the four things.
phrases.notes: Here the 'four things' are the other four payments besides נזק: צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת.

phrases.english: If it was because of a usual wind,
and he caused damage and shame,
he is liable for the four things,
and exempt for the shame.
And if he turned himself over,
phrases.notes: He twisted in the air to land on the person, so his own fall would be softer.

phrases.english: he is liable even for the shame.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling from רבה about a man falling from a roof. It builds on the idea from Step 6 that בושת needs intent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Unusual wind: only נזק. Usual wind: four payments, no בושת. Turned himself over: also בושת.

steps.title: A verse shows that intent to harm is enough for shame payment
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the extra word 'וְהֶחֱזִיקָה' to teach that if someone intended to cause harm, he pays בושת even without intending to shame.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: Since the verse says 'and she put out her hand,' don't I already know she grabbed? Why does it add 'and she grabbed'? To teach that once a person intended to cause damage, he pays for shame even if he did not intend to shame.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source for the last part of רבה's ruling: why the man who turned himself over pays בושת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Putting out a hand already implies grabbing, so the word 'וְהֶחֱזִיקָה' looks extra. The ברייתא learns from it that intent to harm is enough to make a person pay בושת. The man who twisted meant to land on the person, so he pays בושת even though shaming was not his goal.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the verse need to say this?

phrases.english: As it was taught in a ברייתא:
From the implication of what is said,
"and she put out her hand,"
do I not already know that she grabbed hold?!
Why does the verse say "and she grabbed hold"?
To tell you:
once he intended to cause damage,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִתְכַּוֵּין לְבַיֵּישׁ.
phrases.english: even though he did not intend to shame.
phrases.notes: The ending is left unsaid: he still pays for the shame.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the last part of Step 7 (turned over, so he pays בושת).
steps.raayaObject: That someone who intended to harm pays בושת even without intending to shame
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא reading the extra word 'וְהֶחֱזִיקָה' in דברים 25:11
steps.whatToRemember: בושת needs some intent. Intending to harm (or to land on someone) is enough, even without intending to shame.

steps.title: A coal placed on a person's heart or on his garment
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that if someone put a coal on another person's heart and he died, the one who put it there is exempt. If he put it on his garment and it burned, he must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה said: If one placed a hot coal on another person's heart and he died, he is exempt. If he placed it on his garment and it burned, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a new ruling comparing harm to a person's body with harm to his clothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The victim could easily have brushed the coal off himself, so the one who placed it is not held responsible for the death. For the garment, he must pay: the owner may have left it there, counting on getting paid for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, does not have to pay or be punished

phrases.english: And רבה said:
If one placed a coal on another person's heart,
and he died, he is exempt.
On his garment, and it burned, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה: הִנִּיחַ לוֹ גַּחֶלֶת עַל לִבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate ruling from רבה in the same series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coal on the heart, victim died: exempt. Coal on the garment, it burned: liable.

steps.title: רבא shows the coal-on-the-heart ruling comes from a משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבא says both of רבה's coal rulings are already taught in a משנה. For the coal on the heart, he brings the משנה about holding someone in fire or water versus pushing him in.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: We learned both of these rulings. For 'on his heart,' as we learned: If one held another down in fire or water and he could not get out and died, he is liable. If he pushed him into fire or water and he could get out but died anyway, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a source for רבה's first ruling (the coal on the heart). The next step gives the source for the garment ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה separates a victim who could not escape from one who could. A coal on the heart is like being pushed into fire when you can climb out: the victim could have removed it, so the one who put it there is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: We have learned both of them (in a משנה)

phrases.english: רבא said:
We learned both of them.
phrases.notes: Both of רבה's coal rulings: the heart and the garment.

phrases.english: For 'on his heart,' as we learned in a משנה:
If one held him down
in fire or in water,
and he cannot get out from there,
and he died, he is liable.
phrases.notes: Liable here means liable to death as a murderer.

phrases.aramaic: דְּחָפוֹ לְתוֹךְ הָאוּר אוֹ לְתוֹךְ הַמַּיִם,
phrases.english: If he pushed him into fire or into water,
and he could get out from there,
and he died, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the first half of Step 9.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's ruling that one who put a coal on another's heart is exempt
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה separating holding someone in fire or water (cannot escape, liable) from pushing him in (could escape, exempt)
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up a key principle: if the victim could easily have saved himself, the one who started the harm is not held responsible for the death.

steps.title: The garment ruling is already in a משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings the משנה of 'tear my garment, break my jug' as the source for רבה's ruling that one who burns another's garment must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: The garment ruling comes from what we learned: 'Tear my garment' or 'Break my jug': the one who does it is liable. 'On condition that you are exempt': he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his point from step 10. He shows that רבה's second coal ruling, about the garment, is also taught in a משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that even when the owner asks you to tear his garment, you still pay unless he clearly says you are free from paying. So if you burn someone's garment without any permission at all, you certainly pay. That is exactly רבה's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
On condition that you are exempt from paying

steps.whatToRemember: Both of רבה's coal rulings have a source in a משנה. The coal on the heart is exempt, and the coal on the garment must be paid.

phrases.english: His garment: as we learned in a משנה:
phrases.notes: This is the second half of רבא's point: the case where the coal was put on the person's clothing.

phrases.english: "Tear my garment," "Break my jug": he is liable.
"On condition that you are exempt": he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's two-part proof begun in step 10, now for the garment case.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's ruling that one who places a coal on another's garment must pay.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: 'Tear my garment, break my jug': liable; 'on condition to be exempt': exempt.

steps.title: רבה asks about a coal on a slave and on an ox
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks whether a coal placed on another's slave is treated like a coal on a person or like damage to property, and then what the law is for an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה asked: If someone placed a coal on the heart of another man's slave, what is the law? Is the slave treated like a person's body, or like his property? And if you say he is like a body, what about his ox?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה asks a new question that grows out of his two coal rulings. He wants to know which ruling applies to an עבד, and then to a שור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A coal on a person's heart makes the one who put it there exempt, but a coal on property makes him pay. An עבד is a person, but he also belongs to his master like property, so which rule fits? רבה then goes one step further: even if a slave counts as a person, what about an animal like a שור?

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (raised a question he wants settled)
Like his body: treated as a person
Like his property: treated as belongings
If you will say: assuming one answer, a further question follows

phrases.english: Rabba asked:

phrases.aramaic: הִנִּיחַ גַּחֶלֶת עַל לֵב עַבְדּוֹ, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: If he placed a coal on the heart of his slave, what is the law?
phrases.notes: "His slave" means the slave of the other person, not the slave of the one who put the coal there.

phrases.english: Is he considered like his body,
or is he considered like his property?
If you will say he is considered like his body,
what is the law for his ox?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבה's two coal rulings (body exempt, property liable) to ask which applies to a slave and to an ox.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a slave, and then an ox, falls under the 'body' rule (exempt) or the 'property' rule (liable) for a coal placed on them.

steps.title: רבה answers: a slave is like a body, an ox is like property
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers his own question: a slave is treated like a person's body, and an ox is treated like property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then he answered it himself: His slave is like his body. His ox is like his property.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה goes back and answers his own question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The עבד is treated like a person, so the coal-on-the-heart rule applies and the one who placed the coal is exempt. The שור is treated like property, so the one who placed the coal must pay. The difference is that a slave is a person who could remove the coal, but an ox cannot be expected to do that.

keyTerms.meaning: He then resolved it: the asker answers his own question

steps.whatToRemember: For a coal placed on them, an עבד counts like a person (exempt) and a שור counts like property (liable).
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'like his body' does not mean the master's own body. It means the slave is treated as a person, not as an object.

phrases.english: He then resolved it:
His slave is like his body,
his ox is like his property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the two-part question רבה raised in step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A slave is treated like a body (the one who placed the coal is exempt), and an ox is treated like property (he is liable).

steps.title: הדרן: Closing כיצד הרגל
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula marks the end of the second פרק of בבא קמא, כיצד הרגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, כיצד הרגל.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the פרק called כיצד הרגל. The next step starts a new פרק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן is a traditional farewell said at the end of each פרק, showing that the learner hopes to return to it. It adds no new law. It closes the discussion of damage by an animal's foot and related cases.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you: the closing formula of a פרק
"How is the foot…": the name of the second פרק of בבא קמא

phrases.english: We will return to you, "How is the foot"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק after רבה's final ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The second פרק of בבא קמא, כיצד הרגל, is complete.

steps.title: The jug left in the public street
steps.stepSummary: The new פרק opens with a משנה: one who leaves a jug in רשות הרבים. A passerby who trips and breaks it does not pay. If the passerby is hurt by it, the jug's owner pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone put a jug (כד) in the public street. Another person came, tripped on it, and broke it. He does not have to pay. If he got hurt from it, the owner of the jug (חבית) has to pay for his injury.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק begins with a משנה about a jug left in a public place. It gives two rulings: one for when the jug gets broken, and one for when a person gets hurt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one who tripped is פטור, because the jug did not belong in the public street and people are not expected to watch where they step. The jug's owner is the one at fault, so if his jug hurts someone, he pays for the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: One who places or leaves something. This word is also the name of the new פרק
The public domain, such as a street

steps.whatToRemember: Jug in the public street: if someone trips and breaks it, he is פטור. If he gets hurt by it, the jug's owner is חייב.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who places a jug (kad)
in the public domain,
and another came and stumbled on it
and broke it, he is exempt.
And if he was hurt by it,
the owner of the barrel (chavit) is liable for his damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמַּנִּיחַ אֶת הַכַּד בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 14 closed the second פרק. This step opens the third פרק with its first משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who trips on and breaks a jug left in רשות הרבים is פטור. If he is hurt by it, the jug's owner is חייב for his damage.

steps.title: The משנה starts with one word and ends with another
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the משנה begins by calling the vessel a כד and ends by calling it a חבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The משנה started with 'כד' and ended with 'חבית'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is noticing a change in wording inside the משנה. This sets up the next moves, where it will show the same switch in other משניות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It looks strange for one case to use two different words for the same jug. The גמרא raises this as a puzzle about wording, not about the law. It does not answer yet; it first gathers more examples.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an argument about who pays. The rulings of the משנה stay the same. The גמרא is only asking about the choice of words.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It began with a kad,
and ended with a chavit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks closely at the wording of the משנה in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the משנה in step 15
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same jug is called by two different names within one case, which seems inconsistent.

steps.title: A second משנה with the same switch: the barrel and the beam
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes another משנה. It starts with a חבית and ends with a כד, which is the opposite direction of the same switch.
steps.simpleTranslation: We also learned in a משנה: One person was coming with his barrel, and another was coming with his beam. If this one's jug broke on that one's beam, he is פטור. It started with 'חבית' and ended with 'כד'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second example of a משנה that switches between the two words. It is building a pattern before it explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the switch goes the other way: חבית first, then כד. This shows the word change in step 15 is not a one-time slip. It happens in other משניות too.

keyTerms.meaning: And we also learned in a משנה

phrases.english: And we learned also:
this one comes with his barrel
and that one comes with his beam,
the jug of this one was broken
by the beam of that one, he is exempt.
It began with a chavit and ended with a kad!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּתְנַן נָמֵי: זֶה בָּא בְּחָבִיתוֹ וְזֶה בָּא בְּקוֹרָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second משנה that shows the same word switch noticed in step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That משניות regularly switch between כד and חבית within one case
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of one carrying a barrel and another carrying a beam

steps.title: A third משנה with the same switch: wine and honey
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a third משנה, about wine and honey. It begins with a כד of honey and ends with a חבית of honey.
steps.simpleTranslation: We also learned: One person came with his barrel of wine, and another came with his jug of honey. The barrel of honey cracked. The first one poured out his wine and saved the honey in his own barrel. He only gets paid for his work. It started with 'כד' and ended with 'חבית'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third example of the same word switch. This finishes collecting evidence, which sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the honey's vessel is called a כד at first and a חבית later in the same case. Three משניות now show the switch. That strongly suggests the משנה treats the two words as interchangeable.

keyTerms.meaning: His wages, meaning payment for his effort

steps.confusionAlert: Do not get caught up in the law of the honey case, about why he only gets wages. The גמרא quotes it here only to show the word switch.
steps.whatToRemember: Three משניות switch between כד and חבית in the middle of a case. The גמרא has gathered this pattern so it can explain it next.

phrases.english: And we learned also:
this one came with his barrel of wine,
and that one came with his jug of honey;
the barrel of honey cracked,
and this one poured out his wine
and saved the honey into it,
phrases.notes: 'Into it' means into his own barrel, the one he just emptied of wine.

phrases.english: he has only his wages.
It began with a kad and ended with a chavit!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּתְנַן נָמֵי: זֶה בָּא בְּחָבִיתוֹ שֶׁל יַיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third משנה that shows the same word switch, completing the pattern.
steps.raayaObject: That משניות regularly switch between כד and חבית within one case
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the wine barrel and the honey jug

steps.title: רב פפא: The two words mean the same vessel
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא concludes from the three משניות that כד and חבית are the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: A כד is the same as a חבית.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question from step 16, where the משנה switched from כד to חבית. Since the משניות keep switching, the two words must mean the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was that the משנה seemed to change the vessel partway through. Steps 17 and 18 showed the same switch in other משניות, in both directions. רב פפא draws the lesson: the switch is not a mistake, because the words are used for the same vessel.

keyTerms.meaning: a jug, often thought of as a smaller vessel
a barrel or cask, often thought of as a larger vessel

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
A kad is the same as a ḥavit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הַיְינוּ כַּד – הַיְינוּ חָבִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proofs in steps 17 and 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the terms: the two words are interchangeable.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה switched words carelessly, or it is talking about two different vessels.
steps.terutzMaskana: The switch is fine, because כד and חבית refer to the same vessel.

steps.title: What difference does it make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where it makes a practical difference that the two words are the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what does this make a difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב פפא's rule matters in real life. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A rule about word meanings needs a practical result. The גמרא wants to know which real situation depends on whether כד and חבית mean the same thing.

keyTerms.meaning: what practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: For what does it make a difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical result of רב פפא's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In which real case it matters that כד and חבית are the same.

steps.title: It matters for buying and selling
steps.stepSummary: The practical difference is in business deals.
steps.simpleTranslation: For buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that the rule matters when someone buys or sells a vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose a buyer asks for one word and the seller hands over the other vessel. If the words mean the same thing, the buyer cannot say he got the wrong item.

phrases.english: For buying and selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule matters in sales: a buyer who asked for one word cannot complain about receiving the other vessel.

steps.title: In a place where the words are kept apart, the rule is obviously wrong
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case this could be. It cannot be a place where people never mix the two words.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it is a place where people do not call a כד a חבית, and do not call a חבית a כד, then there they simply do not call it that!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's answer by asking where it could apply. In a town where the two words are always kept apart, the rule cannot be true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Business deals follow the way local people talk. If nobody in town uses the two words for the same vessel, a buyer who asked for a חבית clearly did not want a כד. So רב פפא's rule cannot be talking about such a place.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? How exactly does it look?

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say in a place where they do not call a kad a 'ḥavit,'
and they do not call a ḥavit a 'kad,'
but they do not call it that!
phrases.notes: He means: in that town nobody uses one word for the other vessel, so the buyer clearly meant only what he said.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case behind the answer in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that the two words are the same for buying and selling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Sales follow how local people speak. Where people keep the words apart, the rule cannot hold.

steps.title: A town where most people keep the words apart but some mix them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets the case in a mixed town and begins to say what we might have thought there.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a place where most people call a כד a כד and a חבית a חבית, but some people call a חבית a כד and a כד a חבית. You might have said: follow the majority...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by placing רב פפא's rule in a mixed town. It then begins to state what we might have thought there, 'follow the majority.' The sentence finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the case is not obvious. Most people keep the words apart, but a minority use them for the same vessel. The גמרא opens a 'you might have said' line: maybe the sale goes by how most people talk. רב פפא's rule will come to correct that thought.

keyTerms.meaning: no, it is needed for this case
you might have said; introduces a thought the גמרא will reject

steps.confusionAlert: 'Follow the majority' here is what we would have wrongly thought, not the final ruling. The גמרא is setting it up to be rejected on the next amud.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where most call a kad a 'kad'
and a ḥavit a 'ḥavit,'
and there are also those who call a ḥavit a 'kad'
and a kad a 'ḥavit.'
You might have said: go after the majority,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 22 by setting the rule in a mixed town.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule to a specific case: a town where most people keep the words apart and a minority mix them.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We would have followed the majority and treated the words as different.
steps.terutzMaskana: The full conclusion comes on the next amud, after the 'you might have said' line is completed.
